newsitem.title: UK: UK grain market shrugs off green rate change.
newsitem.headline: UK grain market shrugs off green rate change.

text.p: Sterling's green rate revaluation has had no noticeable effect on the UK physical grains market, traders said.
"It's not an input that the market takes to heart," one UK trader said. "Wheat trades independently of any intervention price," he said.
"It does affect the value of (export) refunds, but most people had factored it in to their calculations anyway," another said.

The new UK rate is 0.768177 stg equals one ECU, compared with the previous rate of 0.809915. It takes effect Tuesday. Green rates are used to convert amounts set under EU farm policy in ecu into national currencies.
Most of the UK's crop is feed wheat, which is not eligible for European Union intervention buying in.
"Barley is different, but it's in demand in the big ports, on the basis of Saudi business," the first trader said.
"People look at competitivity versus French, German and Danish supplies," he said. Another trader, specialised in UK exports, put fob UK wheat at six or seven dollars below equivalent French prices.
Falling Scandinavian prices have combined with the strength of sterling to reinforce the current weakness of UK grains prices.

The domestic market is currently quiet, amid a lack of farmer selling. "It's very difficult to buy spot," one trader said. But he felt that farmers would start to come to the market eventually. "Farmers are going to have to crack sometime."

Another reckoned that the green rate change could help bring prices down, because of the psychological effect on farmer thinking. Even though the sterling value of the intervention price should make no difference, it might encourage some farmers to bring grain to market and accept lower prices, she said.
Domestic consumers were happy with current price levels. "Wheat at this price? That's no problem to them. No problem at all," the first trader said.
